title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
The Local and Global Dynamics of Valenced Networks



Relationships are not just present or absent; they carry emotional valence.
Balance Theory is the foundational framework linking:

Local, psychological micro-motives.
Global, macro-structural network patterns (like polarization).

Today we will cover: Dyadic Balance, Signed Graphs, Triadic Balance, Structural Balance, and Clusterability.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Anatomy of Sentiment Networks



Valenced ties are links representing positive (\(+\)) or negative (\(-\)) feelings, evaluations, or behaviors.

Positive valence: Liking, helping, admiring, loving.
Negative valence: Hating, bullying, fighting, distrusting.

A signed graph features a set of vertices \(V\) and two disjoint sets of edges:

Positive links (\(E^+\)) and negative links (\(E^-\)).

These networks represent stable social attitudes rather than fleeting events.
We can represent them with a signed adjacency matrix: \(+1\) for positive ties, \(-1\) for negative ties, \(0\) for no tie.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Fritz Heider’s Dyadic Balance



Developed by social psychologist Fritz Heider (1946) to examine how ties cohere within a single pair.
Distinction between:

Symmetric ties: Relations implied by similarity or co-membership (e.g., sharing a workspace).
Asymmetric ties: Directional sentiments (e.g., liking).

First Proposition: Similarity breeds liking. Sharing co-membership or space breeds positive asymmetric ties (\(aSb \implies aLb\)).
Forms a positive feedback loop: We spend more time with those we like (\(aLb \implies aSb\)).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Proximity, Similarity, and Multiplexity



Over time, people accumulate multiple types of ties, leading to multiplex ties (“multistranded” connections).
Principle of Propinquity (Newcomb 1956): Sharing physical space or social contexts automatically facilitates acquaintance and liking.

Proximity breeds interaction, which breeds similarity, which in turn breeds liking, support, and advice.

Relationships transition from uniplex (single-stranded) to multiplex.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Dyadic Balance and Cognitive Tension



Second Proposition: We strive to maintain positive asymmetric ties with those we are similar to.
Situations where similarity is paired with dislike (\(aSb \land aDb\)) are unbalanced.

Creates cognitive inconsistency and an unpleasant state of affective tension (e.g., hating a forced co-worker).

Resolution of Imbalance:

Break the similarity tie (e.g., quit the job).
Transform the dislike into liking (e.g., adapt to like the co-worker).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Fritz Heider’s P-O-Q Triad



To analyze triads, Heider extended dyadic balance to three distinct elements: the P-O-Q Triad.
Person (P): The focal individual from whose cognitive perspective the triad is analyzed.
Other (O): Towards whom P holds a directed sentiment.
Third Party / Object (Q): Another actor, group, organization, or abstract cultural idea.
Sentiments are modeled via directed, signed edges (\(+\) or \(-\)) going from P to O, P to Q, and O to Q.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Mathematics of Triadic Balance



A triad is balanced if the product of its three edge signs is positive: \[\text{Sign}(P, O) \times \text{Sign}(O, Q) \times \text{Sign}(P, Q) = +1\]
Simplified Identification Rule: A triad is balanced if it has an even number of negative links (exactly zero or two).
Balanced configurations are stable and represent harmonious sentiments, creating no cognitive tension.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Balanced Triads: The 4 Stable Configurations




“A friend of a friend is a friend” (\(+ \times + \times + = +1\))

Example: You (P) and friend (O) both like the same classmate (Q).

“An enemy of an enemy is a friend” (\(- \times - \times + = +1\))

Example: You (P) and ally (Q) form a bond against a mutual rival (O).

“A friend of an enemy is an enemy” (\(- \times + \times - = +1\))

Example: Your rival (O) has a close friend (Q); you start to dislike Q.

“An enemy of a friend is an enemy” (\(+ \times - \times - = +1\))

Example: Your country ally (O) declares war on country (Q); you also oppose Q.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Unbalanced Triads: The 4 Unstable Configurations




“A friend of my friend is my enemy” (\(+ \times + \times - = -1\))

Example: Friend (O) likes (Q), whom you (P) dislike.

“An enemy of a friend is a friend” (\(+ \times - \times + = -1\))

Example: Partner (O) hates Marvel movies (Q), which you (P) love.

“A friend of an enemy is a friend” (\(- \times + \times + = -1\))

Example: You (P) and your rival (O) are both attracted to the same person (Q).

“An enemy of my enemy is also my enemy” (\(- \times - \times - = -1\))

Example: You (P) dislike both the Yankees (O) and Red Sox (Q).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Tension and Change



The basic idea is that unbalanced configurations will tend to transition to balanced configurations.
Unbalanced configurations produce tension in P, leading them to change their sentiments toward O or Q to generate balance.
Balanced configurations are stable equilibrium states.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Cross-Pressure



Because we have multiple social relations, we are sometimes caught between worlds.
This is called cross-pressure.
Example: having two friends with different attitudes towards the same object.
Balance theory predicts that P will have an ambivalent attitude toward the object.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Cross-Pressure in Real-Life: Politics



Political preferences provide a classic illustration of cross-pressure.
Imagine you (P) have a brother (O1) who is a passionate Democrat (\(+\)) and a sister (O2) who strongly opposes them (\(-\)).
Because you have positive bonds with both, you find yourself cross-pressured regarding the Democrats (Q).
This pressure produces social ambivalence, often leading individuals to identify as moderates or independents with no strong partisan affiliation.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Structural Balance at the Network Level
text:
Structural Balance at the Network Level



Balance theory can be scaled up from individual cognitive triads to the whole network level.
This extension is known as Structural Balance Theory.
In its original formulation, it applies to complete signed graphs, where every pair of actors is connected by either a positive or negative link.
In a signed adjacency matrix representation of a signed graph:

Positive links are represented by \(+1\).
Negative links are represented by \(-1\).
Non-adjacent nodes are represented by \(0\).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: The Fundamental Theorem of Structural Balance
text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Structural Balance



The fundamental theorem of structural balance was discovered by the mathematicians Dorwin Cartwright and Frank Harary in 1956.
It states that when a graph is balanced, it can be split into two groups such that there are:

Only positive links within groups.
Only negative links between groups.

Balance is not necessarily good! Structural balance is equivalent to perfect group polarization.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Signed Matrices & Faction Detection



How can we mathematically recover and identify factions in a balanced network?
Rearrange the rows and columns of the signed adjacency matrix such that nodes in the same faction are adjacent.
This permutation yields a block-diagonal signed matrix.
Inside the diagonal blocks, cells are \(+1\) (internal cohesion), whereas off-diagonal blocks are entirely \(-1\) (external conflict).
The 3 × 3 blocks below mirror the two three-person factions in the previous slide’s graph.


Faction Block-Diagonal Matrix
\[M = \begin{pmatrix}
  \begin{array}{ccc|ccc}
    \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & - & - & - \\
    \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & - & - & - \\
    \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & - & - & - \\ \hline
    - & - & - & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} \\
    - & - & - & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} \\
    - & - & - & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+}
  \end{array}
\end{pmatrix}\]

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Cycles and Paths in Balanced Graphs
text:
Cycles and Paths in Balanced Graphs



Partitioning has direct, rigid consequences for paths and cycles in complete graphs:
Cycles: All cycles in a balanced signed graph must have a positive sign product.

Staying inside a group uses only positive links.
Spanning across groups requires crossing the boundary an even number of times, multiplying an even number of negative signs to yield a positive product.

Paths:

Paths ending in the same group have a positive product.
Paths ending in different groups have a negative product (due to odd boundary crossings).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Checking for Balance with Matrix Powers
text:
Checking for Balance with Matrix Powers



How can we test balance in a large network without drawing every cycle?
Raise the signed adjacency matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) to the \(p\)-th power.
Each diagonal entry \(a_{ii}^{(p)}\) sums the sign products of all closed walks of length \(p\) starting and ending at node \(i\).
The test: If the graph is balanced, every diagonal entry of \(\mathbf{A}^p\) is non-negative for all \(p\) up to the number of nodes.
A single negative diagonal entry reveals a negative cycle of length \(p\) — and the graph is unbalanced.


The test in symbols
\[a_{ii}^{(p)} \geq 0 \; \text{for all } i,\; p = 1, \dots, g\]
If any entry is negative:
\[a_{ii}^{(p)} < 0 \implies \text{unbalanced cycle}\]

No need to enumerate cycles — the matrix does the counting.
A practical check for real, messy networks.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Measuring Partial Balance



Real networks are almost never perfectly balanced, so we measure the degree of balance.
Cycle Index of Balance: the share of all cycles whose sign product is positive. \[\text{Cycle Index} = \frac{PC}{TC}\]
Ranges from 0 (completely unbalanced) to 1 (perfectly balanced).
Line Index of Balance (Harary 1959): the minimum number of edge signs that must be flipped to make the graph perfectly balanced.



A large network with a Line Index of 1 or 2 is extremely close to complete balance.
Even when cycle-counting finds dozens of unbalanced cycles, a small Line Index says the polarized structure is nearly there.
Short cycles matter more psychologically, so weighted versions (Henley, Horsfall & De Soto 1969) give triads extra weight.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Directed Balance: Semicycles



Real sentiment ties are often asymmetric — you like someone who dislikes you.
Restricting balance to strict directed cycles (arrows all pointing the same way) would miss most tension: Your friend Alex dislikes Jordan, yet you like both. No directed cycle exists, but the tension is real.
Semipath: a path that ignores arrow direction.
Semicycle: a closed semipath (a cycle in the underlying undirected graph).
A signed digraph is balanced if and only if every semicycle has a positive sign (an even number of negative arcs).



The Cartwright–Harary partition rule carries over unchanged: positive arcs within factions, negative arcs between them.
One rule-violating positive tie across factions injects unbalanced semicycles into the whole network.
This is the directed version of everything we just did with cycles.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Empirical Case Study: Political Blogs



Balanced states describe stable polarization and conflict, not harmony.
Adamic & Glance (2005) examined the hyperlink network of 2004-election political bloggers.
Two highly connected factions (Liberals, Conservatives); dense internal linking, sparse cross-group linking — an echo chamber.
The hyperlink data are unsigned; the figure’s negative ties illustrate the predicted structure, not measured hostility.
Balance explains why polarized factions are stable — and a balanced state need not be a “good” one.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Beyond Two Factions: Davis’s Theorem



Cartwright & Harary’s model splits networks into exactly two opposing factions.
This is too restrictive for many real-world networks, such as school cliques, gangs, or multi-party politics.
In 1967, sociologist James Davis introduced his Clusterability Theorem.
He generalized structural balance so that a network could fragment into any number of distinct clusters (\(k \ge 1\)), rather than just two.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The All-Negative Triad Rule



Classical balance considers a triad with three negative ties (everyone hating everyone else) to be unbalanced.
Davis argued that in highly factionalized contexts, it is perfectly stable for three individuals from completely different, competing groups to dislike one another.
The Clustering Criterion (Davis 1967): A graph is clusterable if and only if it contains no cycle of any length with exactly one negative tie.
For complete graphs this reduces to a triad test: no triad with exactly one negative tie. All-positive, two-negative, and all-negative triads are all permitted.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Ranked Clusterability: Bridging Balance and Hierarchy
text:
Ranked Clusterability: Bridging Balance and Hierarchy



Balance and clusterability both assume horizontal, symmetric sentiment structures.
Real groups often have vertical hierarchies — status, dominance, prestige.
Ranked Clusterability (Davis & Leinhardt 1972): clusters that are themselves hierarchically ordered.

Within clusters: horizontal, positive ties (peer solidarity).
Between clusters: vertical ties. Positive ties point up the hierarchy (deference); negative or null ties point down or across unranked clusters.

This is the mathematical bridge from balance theory to status and dominance hierarchies.



Think of an office: peers are mutual friends, everyone looks up to the executives, discipline flows downward.
Same local logic (no odd cycles of negativity), but the factions are now stacked, not side by side.
Coming up next: theories of valenced interactions, including dominance hierarchies in detail.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Summary: Structural Balance vs. Clusterability



Structural Balance (Cartwright-Harary 1956):

Local rule: Triads cannot have an odd number of negative ties.
Global topology: Splits the network into exactly two factions.

Clusterability (Davis 1967):

Local rule: Relaxes constraints by permitting all-negative triads (no triads with exactly one negative tie).
Global topology: Splits the network into any number of clusters (\(k \ge 1\)).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Dyadic Balance: From Similarities to Interactions
text:
Dyadic Balance: From Similarities to Interactions

Ideas of dyadic balance were first described in a famous paper written by Fritz Heider in 1946.
Ties differ based on whether they are based on:

Similarities.
Interactions.

The basic principle is that people seek balance between similarities and interactions.

People tend to interact with people who are similar to them.

If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are two people, \(S\) is a tie based on similarity and \(R\) is a tie based on interaction:

\[\alpha S \beta \rightarrow \alpha R \beta\]

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Dyadic Balance: Reading the Principle



\(\alpha S \beta \rightarrow \alpha R \beta\) reads: “A tie of type \(S\) between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) leads to a tie of type \(R\) between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).”
This applies to every combination of similarities and interactions.
Examples:

People tend to like the people they spend time with.
People tend to help people who belong to the same groups as them.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: What Counts as Similarities and Interactions?
text:
What Counts as Similarities and Interactions?



Similarities

Propinquity (same place).
Homophily (same social category).
Co-memberships (same social groups).




Interactions

Communicating with.
Liking.
Helping.




Reference: Borgatti, S. P., Mehra, A., Brass, D. J., & Labianca, G. (2009). Network analysis in the social sciences. Science, 323(5916), 892–895.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Worked Example: Spending Time and Liking
text:
Worked Example: Spending Time and Liking



Balanced: Simbi and Keryl spend time together and like each other.

Similarity and interaction point the same way.

Unbalanced: Simbi and Keryl spend time together, but the liking is one-sided.

A similarity paired with a missing or hostile interaction creates tension.

Balance theory predicts the tension gets resolved: the liking becomes mutual, or the time spent together dries up.












Solid green: liking (directed). Blue: spend time with (symmetric).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Worked Example: Same Groups and Helping
text:
Worked Example: Same Groups and Helping



Balanced: Simbi and Keryl belong to the same groups and help each other.
Unbalanced: They share group memberships, but the helping only flows one way.
Same logic, different content: any symmetric similarity tie wants to be matched by reciprocal interaction ties.












Solid green: help (directed). Blue: same group (symmetric).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: The Cycle Runs Both Ways: From Interactions to Similarities
text:
The Cycle Runs Both Ways: From Interactions to Similarities

After the first cycle of similarities leading to interactions, interactions can lead to further similarities: \(\alpha R \beta \rightarrow \alpha S \beta\).
People tend to think like (share the opinions and attitudes of) the people they interact with.
People tend to adopt the same tastes and fashions as the people in the same organizations as them.
People tend to spend time with the people they like.
Similarities and interactions feed each other in a continuing loop.

Signed Graphs

One set of vertices \(V\).
Two disjoint sets of edges:

Positive links (\(E^+\)).
Negative links (\(E^-\)).


The graph is written \(G = \{V, E^+, E^-\}\).
Two sets are disjoint when they don’t share any members (their intersection is the empty set \(\emptyset\)).
Signed graphs can be either directed or undirected.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Balance Theory

Balance theory is a social psychological theory designed to explain expected triadic configurations in sentiment networks.
Sentiment networks are built from valenced ties (e.g., positive or negative).
There are four building blocks in balance theory.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Building Block 1: A Person (P)



The person (P).
We “look” at the triad from this person’s point of view.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Building Block 2: An Object (O)



An object (O) towards which the focal person has some kind of sentiment.
The sentiment can be positive or negative.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Building Block 3: A Third Party (Q)



A third party (Q) towards which both the person and the other also have some kind of sentiment.
Q does not have to be a real person! It could be any object.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Building Block 4: Directed Signed Edges



A set of directed signed edges indicating positive (solid green) or negative (dashed red) sentiments:

From P to O.
From P to Q.
From O to Q.

This configuration reads: Person (P) likes Other (O); Other (O) likes the third party (Q); but Person (P) dislikes the third party.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Triad in Everyday Terms












Sounds dicey!
You (P) have a friend (O) who likes another classmate (Q) whom you dislike.












Everything’s fine!
You (P) have a friend (O) who likes another classmate (Q) whom you also like.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Triad in Everyday Terms (continued)












Seems fine?
You (P) have an enemy (O) who likes another classmate (Q) whom you also dislike.












Trouble in paradise!
You (P) love Marvel movies (Q), but your long-time partner O (whom you like, duh!) hates them.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Eight Configurations

There are eight (8) configurations, featuring one-way directed links from:

Person (P) to Other (O).
Person (P) to Third Party (Q).
Other (O) to Third Party (Q).

Four of them are balanced; four are unbalanced.

Balanced Configurations

“A friend of a friend is a friend.”
“An enemy of an enemy is a friend.”
“A friend of an enemy is an enemy.”
“An enemy of a friend is an enemy.”

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Unbalanced Configurations













In each unbalanced configuration, the sentiments collide.
“A friend of my friend is my enemy.”
“An enemy of a friend is a friend.”
“A friend of an enemy is a friend.”
“An enemy of my enemy is also my enemy.”

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
The Mathematics of Balance Theory

Remember the rules of sign multiplication from basic algebra?

\[+1 \times +1 = +1 \qquad +1 \times -1 = -1 \qquad -1 \times -1 = +1\]

They apply to balance theory!

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Unbalanced Triads Have a Negative Product
text:
Unbalanced Triads Have a Negative Product













If you multiply the signs of the edges of each unbalanced triad, you get a negative number. Try it!
\((+1_{PO}) \times (+1_{OQ}) \times (-1_{PQ}) = -1_{POQ}\)
\((+1_{PO}) \times (-1_{OQ}) \times (+1_{PQ}) = -1_{POQ}\)
\((-1_{PO}) \times (+1_{OQ}) \times (+1_{PQ}) = -1_{POQ}\)
\((-1_{PO}) \times (-1_{OQ}) \times (-1_{PQ}) = -1_{POQ}\)

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: Balanced Triads Have a Positive Product
text:
Balanced Triads Have a Positive Product













Conversely, if you multiply the signs of the edges of each balanced triad, you get a positive number.
\((-1_{PO}) \times (+1_{OQ}) \times (-1_{PQ}) = +1_{POQ}\)
\((+1_{PO}) \times (-1_{OQ}) \times (-1_{PQ}) = +1_{POQ}\)
\((-1_{PO}) \times (-1_{OQ}) \times (+1_{PQ}) = +1_{POQ}\)
\((+1_{PO}) \times (+1_{OQ}) \times (+1_{PQ}) = +1_{POQ}\)

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
section: A Link Between Mathematics and the Logic of Social Relations
text:
A Link Between Mathematics and the Logic of Social Relations

“A friend of a friend is a friend”: \(+1_{PO} \times +1_{OQ} \times +1_{PQ} = +1_{POQ}\)
“An enemy of an enemy is a friend”: \(-1_{PO} \times -1_{OQ} \times +1_{PQ} = +1_{POQ}\)
“A friend of an enemy is an enemy”: \(-1_{PO} \times +1_{OQ} \times -1_{PQ} = +1_{POQ}\)
“An enemy of a friend is an enemy”: \(+1_{PO} \times -1_{OQ} \times -1_{PQ} = +1_{POQ}\)
Every folk rule for balanced sentiment is a sign product equal to \(+1\).

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs
text:
Resolving Cross-Pressure



To achieve balance and remove the ambivalence, P can:

Change their own attitude toward Friend 1 or Friend 2.
Convince either Friend 1 or Friend 2 to change their attitude toward the object.

The same tension-and-resolution logic that works triad by triad also works for whole networks. That is where we go next.

title: Balance Theory and Signed Graphs

From Triadic Balance to Structural Balance

If a triad is balanced, then it is so from every member’s point of view.
We just need to change the interpretation!
Take this balanced triad and rotate the “you” position around the triangle.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Introduction to Valenced Interactions
Beyond Simple Co-membership



In social network analysis, we move beyond simple presence or absence of links to examine sentiment networks.
Relationships have an emotional and evaluative character, labeled as valence:

Positive valence (e.g., liking, helping, admiring).
Negative valence (e.g., disliking, bullying, fighting).

Valenced Interactions are governed by deep-seated psychological micro-motives.
These principles drive how networks grow, change, and cohere into stable macrostructures.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Karma Theory: Core Concept
What You Send Out Predicts What You Get Back



Core Principle: “You get what you spread out!”
The valence of the ties you send out predicts the valence of the ties you receive back — from the network at large, not necessarily from the same alter.
Predicts received valenced indegree (what you receive) based on expressed valenced outdegree (what you send out).
Illustrates common expressions:

“Likers get liked” (positive).
“Bullies get bullied” (negative).

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Karma Theory: Network-Wide Flow



Karma Flows can be generalized across broader spheres in the network.
Positive Sphere: Node A (positive spreader) actively initiates friendly ties and receives deference/support in return from the network.
Negative Sphere: Node B (negative spreader) actively initiates hostile ties and attracts reciprocal conflict/bullying from multiple alters.
No alter returns a tie directly; the match is between what each sends and what it receives from others.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
section: Karma Dynamics: Virtuous vs. Vicious Cycles
text:
Karma Dynamics: Virtuous vs. Vicious Cycles



Karma principles drive valenced networks to grow and evolve via feedback loops:
Virtuous Cycles: An initial positive act (\(+\)) breeds matching positive sentiment from others (\(+\)) — not necessarily from the same alter. These positive feedback loops lock actors into mutually reinforcing, cooperative cliques.
Vicious Cycles: A single unprovoked negative act (\(-\)) breeds hostile counter-attacks (\(-\)). This triggers cascading negative spirals, spreading localized conflict throughout the network.
Over time, outdegree and received indegree valences converge on a node-by-node basis.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Status Theory: Introduction



Status Theory proposes that sentiments towards an alter are heavily driven by how others feel about them.
It extends the triadic balance logic from the previous lecture.
This represents a social prestige alignment mechanism:

If someone is liked by many, you align your sentiment and like them too.
If someone is disliked by many, you align your sentiment and dislike them.

A node’s status is determined by the valence signs of incoming ties:

High status = receiving many positive links.
Low status = receiving many negative links.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Prestige and Deference Alignment



Inside status-seeking systems, tie directions carry implicit status expectations:

Directed positive tie from Ego to Alter \(\implies\) Ego considers Alter to have higher status (Deference).
Directed negative tie from Ego to Alter \(\implies\) Ego considers Alter to have lower status (Dominance).

Status-seeking actors strive to align their sentiments with prestige to avoid losing their own social standing.

text:
Status and Outgoing Sentiments



Your outgoing ties affect your own social position:

Status Gain:

Sending positive ties to high-status actors (basking in reflected glory).
Sending negative ties to low-status actors (distancing from pariahs).

Status Loss:

Sending positive ties to low-status actors (guilt by association).
Sending negative ties to high-status actors (hostility to elites backfires).


Actors actively prune or withdraw ties that cause status loss.

section: Status Dynamics: Centralization and Hierarchy Growth
text:
Status Dynamics: Centralization and Hierarchy Growth



How status networks grow and change over time:

Preferential Deference: High-status nodes attract a disproportionate share of incoming positive ties over time (a “rich-get-richer” effect).
Dynamic Pruning: High-status nodes lose their negative ties, while low-status nodes lose their positive ties.
“Gang-up” Effect: Subordinates consolidate negative ties onto low-status pariahs to boost their own standings.
Hierarchy Emergence: Sentiments organize into highly centralized, strictly ordered prestige rankings.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Solidarity Theory: Core Concept



Central idea: “People in the same position in the valenced interaction network are likely to link via positive ties.”
Time 1: Ego and Other already occupy the same position — each sends (+) and receives (+) ties from distinct alters (the popular “in-crowd”).
Time 2: The shared position generates a new positive tie between them — status solidarity: “Cool kids stick together!”

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Measuring Shared Position



Structural similarity acts as a strong motivator for positive bonding:

Status Solidarity: Elite, popular actors share a similar high status, motivating them to like and support one another (“popular kids stick together”).
Unpopularity Solidarity: Disliked, downtrodden actors share a similar lower-tier position, motivating them to bond (“downtrodden stick together”).
Vertical Cleavages: Since different positions motivate negative sentiments, positive ties spanning across tiers are actively pruned.

section: Solidarity Dynamics: Stratification and Clique Growth
text:
Solidarity Dynamics: Stratification and Clique Growth



How Solidarity networks grow and stratify over time:

Horizontal Integration: Sharing the same status position drives the creation of reciprocal positive ties within the same tier (clique formation).
Class Cohesion: Solidarity processes stabilize clusters into horizontal social classes (e.g., unions, associations, exclusive clubs).
Vertical Hostility: Cross-tier bonding is severed. What remains across tiers is asymmetric — deference flowing up to the elite, dominance flowing down.
Clique Stratification: The network evolves into a horizontally integrated, vertically polarized system.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
section: Dominance Orders in the Animal Kingdom
text:
Dominance Orders in the Animal Kingdom



Dominance hierarchies are observed across many species — most notably among chickens. No big brain needed to build a complex social network!
A “pure” dominance order has three algebraic properties:

Directed: a tie means “i dominates j.”
Antisymmetric: if A dominates B, B cannot dominate A.
Complete: for every pair, someone dominates — either A dominates B or B dominates A.












One tie per pair (antisymmetric, complete) — but arranged as a cycle, which a pure dominance order cannot contain.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Transitivity in Dominance Orders



Transitivity: dominance passes through nodes.
If A dominates B, and B dominates C, then A also dominates C — just like \(A > B\) and \(B > C\) imply \(A > C\).
In a directed network: if A is above B, A is above everyone B is above.
A linear dominance order must be transitive — the A → C arc has to exist.
An intransitive triad has the full chain A → B → C but the A → C tie reversed (C → A) — the closure is contradicted, not merely absent.
A merely absent A → C tie is a different case, the pass-along triad, which we return to below.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Vacuous Transitivity



What if A → B, but B does not direct a tie to C?
The precondition for transitivity — A → B and B → C — is not met.
The triad cannot violate transitivity, because the necessary chain does not exist.
This configuration is vacuously transitive:

It does not actively demonstrate transitivity…
…but it does not violate it either.

Only triads with a full chain A → B → C can be transitive or intransitive.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
section: Perfectly Linear Hierarchies: The Pecking Order
text:
Perfectly Linear Hierarchies: The Pecking Order













Chickens placed in a new environment scuffle until a clear pecking order emerges.
The winner asserts dominance; this continues until every chicken knows its place.
Alpha dominates Beta and everyone below; Beta dominates Gamma and everyone below, and so on.
The hierarchy is ritually reinforced: the higher-status chicken pecks, the lower-status one assents.
A classic perfectly transitive dominance order.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
section: Human Hierarchies: Deviations from Perfect Transitivity
text:
Human Hierarchies: Deviations from Perfect Transitivity



Unlike chickens, human hierarchies are typically not perfectly transitive — and they vary by context.
A teacher has final authority in the classroom, but those relations may not apply outside it.
Deference to a President can invert during an election — the position depends on the voters’ will.
Two people can each lead in different clubs; their relative standing shifts with the decision at hand.
Humans tacitly recognize orderings, but disagreements over what determines status arise, and hierarchies are context-dependent.



Human hierarchies still tend toward the linear ideal:

Deviations are often temporary or local.
Ambiguity about the order itself breeds conflict and competition.

Still, human networks can be analyzed by comparing them to these idealized structures.

A dominance network can contain seven possible triadic configurations built entirely of asymmetric or null ties.
For a linear order to exist, it must be transitive and contain no cyclical triads.
Everything except the cycle is compatible with a linear order; the pass-along triad simply has not yet resolved its A–C tie.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
section: Models of Hierarchy Formation: The Attribute-Based Model
text:
Models of Hierarchy Formation: The Attribute-Based Model



Attribute-based model: position in the hierarchy reflects inherent qualities and abilities — talent, athletic ability, humor, being a good friend all count as “quality” — with the “biggest, fastest, strongest” rising to the top.
Deference does the compensating (Gould 2002):

A less talented person “exchanges” deference for association with a more talented one.
Yielding signals the recipient’s quality and status, increasing their influence.

If required deference exceeds the acceptable limits of reciprocity, the tie may not form at all.
Implication: a relatively stable hierarchy mirroring underlying capabilities.



But is rank really just a readout of attributes?
Enter the interaction-based model…

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
The Interaction-Based Model: Agonistic Competition













Interaction-based model (Chase 1982): hierarchies emerge from the sequence and outcomes of past agonistic encounters — not only from attributes.
Winner effects: winning brings confidence, experience, testosterone — winners dominate again (double-dominant triads).
Loser effects: losing brings lowered confidence and injury — losers lose again (double-loser triads).
Bystander effects: observers update from watching:

A bystander defers to the winner and rarely dominates them.
But a bystander becomes stronger relative to the loser, and rarely gets dominated by them.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Bystander Effects: A Worked Example



Three chickens: A is strong, B is moderately strong, C is weak.
A fights and defeats B — which suffers injury and lost confidence.
C only watched. Yet it can now defeat B, something it could not do before.
C’s new tie is a bystander update. It never fought A, and it never beat B before.
The final hierarchy is not a readout of abilities alone; it is shaped by the order in which contests occur.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Why Iterative Competition Guarantees Linearity

Combine the three effects over repeated contests:

Winners keep winning; losers keep losing (double-dominant and double-loser triads).
Bystanders almost never dominate the initial dominant — and almost never get dominated by the initial loser.

Bystander updating therefore locks in the outcome of every observed fight rather than reversing it.
Step by step, every triad that could be cyclical or intransitive gets resolved toward transitivity.
The resulting hierarchy is not a pure readout of attributes: it is shaped by the history and sequence of interactions.
Iterative, social competition pushes the dominance order strongly toward transitivity and linearity over time — the model’s prediction, even if real human hierarchies only approximate it.

Compare how distinct social-psychological principles drive micro-motives.
Each theory assumes different levels of agency and structural awareness:

Karma: Matches the valence a node sends with the valence it receives — from the network, not dyad by dyad.
Status: Aligns sentiments with prestige hierarchies (prestige seeking).
Solidarity: Aligns sentiments with others in the same status position (horizontal classes).

section: Co-Evolution of Valenced Networks: A Combined Model
text:
Co-Evolution of Valenced Networks: A Combined Model



In real-world sentiment networks, these three principles do not act in isolation; they interact and co-evolve:

Phase 1: Raw Interaction: Initial encounters are governed by Karma (direct reciprocity loops).
Phase 2: Hierarchy Emergence: As actors seek status and prestige, Status seeking creates centralized deference paths.
Phase 3: Factional Stratification: Sharing the same status position triggers Solidarity, freezing actors into cohesive horizontal classes.

Dominance (Part 4) adds a fourth dynamic, agonistic competition, on top of these — an illustrative synthesis, not a chapter claim.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
Solidarity on the Negative Side



The same logic holds at the bottom of the status order: actors who send and receive negative ties cluster together.
Shared unpopularity motivates bonding among the downtrodden (“misery loves company”).
Negative-sphere clusters mirror the positive-sphere cliques — solidarity built out of shared hostile exchange.

title: Chains of Affection
text:
Why Study Romantic & Sexual Networks?

The Closed Laboratory:

Unlike abstract communities, school-based dating and sexual networks are bounded settings with high social visibility.
Individual relationship preferences are intimate, dyadic choices, but when aggregated, they form a global network structure.

The Core Paradox:

Individual actors have zero awareness of the global structure.
No adolescent says: “I will date this person to maximize network centralization.”
Yet, by following simple, local micro-level rules, individuals generate elegant, system-wide macro-level patterns.

title: Chains of Affection
text:
Macro-Structures & Disease Diffusion

The Stakes of Topology:

The path layout of a network determines how rapidly pathogens (like STIs/HIV) can travel.
The Core Model: Densely connected clusters or pockets of high-risk actors. Highly resilient to intervention.
The Spanning Tree: Long, thin, fragile chains with very few shortcuts (cycles). Extremely vulnerable to random interventions.

The Micro-Macro Link:

By understanding the unwritten local rules of adolescent society, we can predict—and break—the path of disease transmission.

title: Chains of Affection
text:
The “Chains of Affection” Discovery



Peter Bearman, James Moody, and Katherine Stovel (2004):

Conducted a landmark study of “Jefferson High” (832 students).

The Global Finding:

Found a massive spanning tree structure!
Over 52% of active students were linked in a single giant, chain-like component.
It had almost zero cycles (redundant loops), resembling rural telephone wires stretching from a single main trunk.

Why is this a puzzle?

Standard social preferences like homophily (dating similar people) predict highly clustered, dense, closed pockets—not long, fragile chains!



Spanning Tree Chain

title: Chains of Affection
text:
The 4-Cycle Proscription: The Tabooed Loop


The Micro-Level Proscription: “You do not date your ex’s current partner’s ex” (avoiding seconds partnerships) — completing the loop costs a public loss of status.
Bearman et al. found only two 4-cycles in the entire school, vastly fewer than expected by random chance.












Time 1: Mateo dates Priya, while Devin dates Mei.
Time 2: After breakups, Priya and Devin start dating.
Time 3: Mateo and Mei dating would complete the forbidden 4-cycle loop — so they avoid each other!

title: Chains of Affection
section: The Power of a Negative Rule
text:
The Power of a Negative Rule



Spanning Trees are Born from Proscriptions:

Spanning trees (chain-like structures) are not generated by positive choices, but by negative rules (what you cannot do).
Like incest taboos in kinship networks, the prohibition against completing short cycles forces individuals to look outward.

The Spanning Result:

By refusing to close the loop, Mateo and Mei must find partners outside their immediate circle.
This simple choice stretches the network out into long, fragile chains.














Forcing Mateo and Mei to look outward stretches the tree!

title: Chains of Affection
text:
“Keeping to the Code” (McMillan et al., 2022)

The Critique of the Classic Taboo:

McMillan, Kreager, and Veenstra (2022) argue that Bearman’s norm lacks face validity.
No high schooler actually thinks in terms of: “Is this my ex-partner’s current partner’s ex-partner?”
It is too abstract and unarticulated.

The Alternative Multi-Relational Norm:

Romantic relationships are embedded in a dense peer friendship network.
The actual micro-level rule is: The “No Seconds” Friendship Code (colloquially, “Girl Code” or “Bro Code”).
“Do not date your friend’s previous romantic partner.”

title: Chains of Affection
text:
Visualizing the Friendship Code Process

How same-sex loyalty blocks the 4-cycle loop step-by-step:













Phase 1: Marcus dates Sofia; Marcus is friends with Kenji, Sofia with Maya.
Phase 2: Double-dating creates friendly ties: Marcus–Maya and Sofia–Kenji.
Phase 3 (Breakup): Loyalty wins — Kenji never dates Marcus’s ex, Maya never dates Sofia’s ex; the 4-cycle is blocked, splitting the group into two chains!

title: Chains of Affection
text:
Empirical Evidence of the Code

Testing the PEAR Study Network:

McMillan et al. studied a Dutch high school romantic network (607 students).
Adhered to Bearman’s spanning tree characteristics: exceptionally sparse (density = 0.005), low cycles (only 8 four-cycles total).

Statistical Network Analysis:

Using advanced statistical models to control for other factors (like popularity, school size, and opportunities), researchers found that the “no seconds” Girl/Bro Code is a powerful social rule.
Adolescents are significantly less likely to date their friend’s ex-partner.
In fact, once this friendship loyalty rule is accounted for, there is no other special dating rule needed to explain why 4-cycles are so rare!

Takeaway:

The global spanning tree is not born of a dating-only taboo, but of peer friendship loyalty blocking cycle closure!

title: Chains of Affection
section: Do Fictional Networks Follow the Rules?
text:
Do Fictional Networks Follow the Rules?

Writers of popular television dramas (sitcoms, prime-time soap operas) rely heavily on romantic networks to build storylines.
Let’s examine two famous fictional cases:

Glee’s McKinley High (Seasons 1-2, studied by Jimi Adams, 2015).
Grey’s Anatomy (GAN, Seasons 1-6, studied by Marcum et al., 2016).




The Macro-Observation:

In Glee, a whopping 42% of observed romantic ties are part of a 4-cycle loop (e.g., Quinn-Finn-Rachel-Puckerman).
In Grey’s Anatomy, 4-cycles, love triangles, and overlapping loops are rampant.
Why? Drama needs conflict! Writers actively violate local cycle-avoidance taboos to generate plot tension.

title: Chains of Affection
text:
Glee’s McKinley High Network



High-Clustering Drama:

Glee’s network is incredibly small, highly dense, and saturated with loops.
Screenwriters use cycle completions (e.g., dating a friend’s ex or partner’s ex) to drive dramatic friction.

Statistical Network Models:

When researchers used statistical models controlling for basic features (like how small and active the cast is), fictional characters still exhibit a strong, significant aversion to 4-cycles.
Even under dramatic pressures, scriptwriters implicitly follow real-world sexual taboos.

Takeaway: Fictional networks reproduce real-world avoidance patterns — even without conscious modeling.


Glee’s Saturated Loops

title: Chains of Affection
text:
Heteronormativity vs. Homosexual Markets

Marcum, Lin, and Koehly (2016) extended the study of 4-cycles to homosexual networks, comparing:

Grey’s Anatomy (GAN): Predominantly heterosexual adult network.
Showtime’s The L Word (LWN): Predominantly lesbian same-sex network in Los Angeles.




The Structural Findings:

Heterosexual networks (Grey’s Anatomy, and the real-world Colorado Springs gonorrhea network) show a strong, significant aversion to 4-cycles (they are heavily avoided).
Homosexual networks (The L Word) show no such aversion to 4-cycles (they occur at normal, expected rates).
Love triangles and cycles of length 4 are structurally unconstrained and socially permitted in the lesbian network.

title: Chains of Affection
text:
Market Size and Structural Necessity



Why are same-sex cycles different?
1. Structural Constraint:

Same-sex dating markets are significantly smaller and more constrained than heterosexual markets.
Due to limited partner availability, strict cycle avoidance (the “no seconds” code) would result in a massive proportion of the population being locked out of dating entirely.

2. Normative Shift:

In lesbian same-sex networks, “love triangles” and cycle-closures are normalized.
Gaps are closed out of structural necessity, making cycle-taboos a luxury of large, heteronormative dating pools.

title: Chains of Affection
text:
The Structural Impossibility of Heterosexual 3-Cycles

What is a 3-Cycle?

A closed loop of length 3 where person A dates B, B dates C, and C dates A (the classic “love triangle”).

The Bipartite Rule:

In a strictly heterosexual network, ties only occur between opposite sexes (Boy \(\leftrightarrow\) Girl).
Therefore, heterosexual networks are bipartite graphs, which mathematically can only have even-length cycles (4, 6, 8, etc.).

title: Chains of Affection
section: Closing the Triangle Requires a Same-Sex Tie
text:
Closing the Triangle Requires a Same-Sex Tie

The Catch:

A romantic 3-cycle is structurally impossible in a strictly heterosexual market!
To close a 3-cycle, at least one same-sex (homosexual or bisexual) relationship is mathematically required.














Left: The heterosexual triad cannot close — Kenji and Marcus dating is impossible.
Right: A same-sex tie (Marcus-Kenji, shown in purple) closes the triangle, creating a 3-cycle.

title: Chains of Affection
text:
Allegations of Affection

Carmella Nicole Stoddard’s (2024) UCLA dissertation looked at a massive celebrity dating network scraped from whosdatedwho.com (WDW):

109,626 nodes and 88,746 edges across celebrity histories.

The Core Distinction:

Confirmed Ties: Fully established, mutually acknowledged relationships.
Rumored Ties: Unconfirmed allegations, gossip, and media speculations (3,848 ties).

The Question:

How do rumored ties differ from confirmed ties structurally, and what do they tell us about social norms?

title: Chains of Affection
text:
Visualizing Rumors vs. Reality



Confirmed Structure:

Only opposite-sex confirmed ties exist (Tom Holland \(\leftrightarrow\) Zendaya \(\leftrightarrow\) Timothée \(\leftrightarrow\) Kylie Jenner).
Forms a clean, acyclic tree with zero cycles and strictly heterosexual behavior.

Rumored Structure:

4-Cycle Closure: A rumor that Kylie Jenner dated Tom Holland (red dashed line) closes a 4-cycle loop.
Discordant Sexuality: A rumor that Zendaya dated Kylie Jenner (purple dashed line) is a same-sex tie, suggesting bisexual behavior for both.


























Gossip highlights norm violations by closing cycles (red) and implying bisexuality (purple)!

title: Chains of Affection
text:
Gossip as a Norm-Enforcement Tool

The Tradeoff of Gossip & Rumor:

Gossip is attracted to salaciousness (violations of cycle avoidance, sexuality discordant pairings, extreme age-gaps).
By rumor-mongering these violations (completing 3-cycles and 4-cycles), the community publicly highlights and sanctions deviant behaviors.

The WDW Findings:

Rumored ties are heavily overrepresented in short cycles and age-gapped ties.
Rather than being random noise, rumors are a multiplex tool used to enforce local monogamy and age-homophily norms by shining a spotlight on those who break them.

title: Chains of Affection
section: Summary of the Micro-Macro Romantic Link
text:
Summary of the Micro-Macro Romantic Link

1. Structure Emerges from Gaps:

Spanning tree networks are not created by positive choices, but by negative proscriptions (avoiding short cycles).

2. Friendship Drives Romantic Structures:

The “Bro/Girl Code” (avoiding dating a friend’s ex) is the true local engine that shapes adolescent spanning trees.

3. Market Size Decouples Norms:

Smaller same-sex dating markets cannot afford cycle-avoidance taboos, showing how structural constraints alter social codes.

4. Gossip Maps Deviance:

Celebrity rumor networks demonstrate that gossip serves to identify, broadcast, and sanction those who violate local network taboos.

title: Chains of Affection
text:
Discussion Questions

Why do you think friendship-loyalty norms (“Bro Code” / “Girl Code”) have higher face validity for teenagers than dating-only cycle-avoidance rules?
If same-sex markets must relax cycle-avoidance taboos due to structural constraint, how might this impact the spread of infectious pathogens (STIs) within gay/lesbian communities compared to heterosexual ones?
How does celebrity gossip on sites like whosdatedwho.com act as a “surveillant filter” for norm violations, and what other online communities use rumor as a tool for social control?

text:
Using edge connectivity to find cohesive subsets

We can use pairwise edge connectivity \(\lambda(u, v)\) to recursively find Lambda Sets (Borgatti, Everett, & Shirey, 1990).
The core property of lambda sets:

The pairwise edge connectivity between nodes inside a lambda set is always strictly larger than the edge connectivity between any node inside the set and any node outside the set.
This mathematically guarantees that group members have stronger indirect ties with each other than with any outsider!

Let’s walk through the hierarchical partition algorithm on a 16-node graph.

text:
Lambda sets: step-by-step splitting (cont.)



Step 3: remove \(\{HJ, HM\}\). This disconnects the giant component, yielding a new component and a clique of size 4.

title: Graph Theory: Sub-Groups & Cliques
text:
Lambda sets: step-by-step splitting (cont.)



Step 4: remove \(\{JN, IN\}\). Disconnecting the final component reveals four cohesive subgroups of size 4 — three are cliques, and \(\{I, J, K, L\}\) is missing only the \(IL\) tie (but its members remain far more connected to each other than to outsiders).

text:

Because lambda sets are hierarchically nested, we can plot their nested relationship using a dendrogram.
Properties of lambda sets:

At any given partition height, each node belongs to exactly one lambda set.
Smaller, tighter lambda sets are cleanly nested within larger, looser ones.
Excellent for showing multi-level nested structures (e.g., departments nested in divisions, nested in the firm).

text:
Summary of key terms (I)

Subgraph: A subset (\(G'\)) of the node and the edge set of a graph (\(G\))
Connected subgraph: All nodes in the subgraph can reach other nodes in the subgraph via some path within the subset of edges
Maximal subgraph: A subgraph is maximal with respect to property \(p\) (e.g., completeness, connectivity) when no more nodes or edges can be added to the subgraph without losing that property

Maximally connected subgraph, maximally complete subgraph, etc.

Clique: Maximally complete subgraph
Clique size: Number of nodes in a clique
\(n\)-Clique: A subgraph in which every node can reach every other node inside the subgraph via a path of at most \(n\) steps

title: Graph Theory: Sub-Groups & Cliques
text:
Summary of key terms (II)

Connected graph: All nodes in the graph can reach every other node via a path regardless of length (\(l < \infty\))
Disconnected graph: Some nodes in the graph cannot reach other nodes via any path (e.g., for at least one pair of nodes \(l_{uv} = \infty\))
Components: Maximally connected subgraphs inside a disconnected graph
Giant component: The maximally connected subgraph in a disconnected graph with the largest number of nodes
\(k\)-Connected component: A component that remains connected after the removal of any \(k-1\) nodes (its node connectivity is \(k\))

title: Graph Theory: Sub-Groups & Cliques
text:
Summary of key terms (III)

Bridges: An edge that if it were removed would disconnect the graph
Edge cutset: Minimum number of edges whose removal would disconnect the graph
Node cutset: Minimum number of nodes whose removal would disconnect the graph
uv-cutset: Number of nodes whose removal would disconnect a pair of nodes (\(uv\))
Menger’s theorem: If a graph has \(k\)-connectivity \(= n\), every pair of non-adjacent nodes is connected by at least \(n\) node-independent paths
Cohesive blocking: A way to find densely connected subgroups in a graph by removing nodes in the node cutset (Moody & White 2003)

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
The Position Approach

In social network analysis, we can partition nodes using two different philosophies:

The Group Approach: Nodes are divided into subsets that are tightly interconnected with one another.
The Positional Approach: Nodes are divided into subsets based on how similar they are in their patterns of connectivity with others.

Nodes in the same positional class are said to occupy the same position or role in the social structure.
We distinguish between:

Structural Equivalence: Nodes are connected to the exact same other nodes.
Regular Equivalence: Nodes are connected to equivalent others (e.g., all teachers are connected to students, even if they are different students).

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:

Two nodes are structurally equivalent if they are connected to the same other nodes.
Their patterns of connectivity are mathematically identical.
In the graph on the right:

\(\{C, D\}\) are structurally equivalent because both are connected to \(\{A, B, E\}\).
\(\{A, B\}\) are structurally equivalent because both are connected to \(\{C, D\}\).
\(\{E\}\) and \(\{F\}\) occupy unique positions (neighborhoods are not shared).

text:
Structural Similarity: A Necessary Relaxation

In real-world social networks, strict structural equivalence is extremely rare.

It only allows a binary “yes” or “no” answer: either nodes connect to the exact same neighbors, or they do not.
If node \(A\) and node \(B\) share 99 out of 100 neighbors, they are technically not structurally equivalent!

Structural Similarity:

Allows for a “more or less” gradient rather than binary classification.
Measures the extent to which two nodes have highly overlapping patterns of connectivity.
Let’s look at how we measure this.

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
Euclidean Distance (\(d^{Euclid}_{k,l}\))

Ronald Burt (1976) proposed measuring structural similarity by calculating the Euclidean Distance between the row vectors of nodes in the adjacency matrix.
For nodes \(k\) and \(l\), the distance is:

\[d^{Euclid}_{k,l} = \sqrt{\sum_j (a_{(k)j} - a_{(l)j})^2}\]

Key Properties:

If nodes are structurally equivalent, their Euclidean distance is exactly zero.
The larger the distance, the less structurally similar the two nodes are.

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
Euclidean Distance in Directed Graphs

When networks contain asymmetric (directed) ties, we must distinguish between two behaviors:

Sending Ties: Do nodes \(u\) and \(v\) point to the same out-neighbors? (Row similarity)
Receiving Ties: Do nodes \(u\) and \(v\) receive ties from the same in-neighbors? (Column similarity)

Two directed nodes are structurally equivalent if and only if they send ties to the same others and receive ties from the same others.
The Euclidean distance formula expands to sum both row and column differences:

\[d^{Euclidean}_{k,l} = \sqrt{\sum_j (a_{(k)j}-a_{(l)j})^2 + \sum_i (a_{(k)i}-a_{(l)i})^2}\]

\(\{E, G\}\) are structurally equivalent (\(d_{E, G} = 0\)). They send ties to \(\{C, F\}\) and receive ties from \(\{D\}\).

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
The Intuition of Neighborhood Overlap

Recall that the neighborhood of a node is the set of all other nodes adjacent to it.
Neighborhood Overlap:

The more neighbors two nodes have in common, the more structurally similar they are.
If you and your colleague share 100% of your friends, you are structurally equivalent.
If you share none of your friends, you occupy completely different social worlds.

We can formalize this overlap using three classical set-theoretic coefficients.

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
Three Classical Coefficients

Let \(n_{ij}\) be the number of common neighbors of nodes \(i\) and \(j\); let \(k_i\) and \(k_j\) be their degrees.



1. Jaccard Similarity
\[J_{ij} = \frac{n_{ij}}{k_i + k_j - n_{ij}}\]

2. Dice Similarity
\[D_{ij} = \frac{2n_{ij}}{k_i + k_j}\]

3. Cosine Similarity
\[C_{ij} = \frac{n_{ij}}{\sqrt{k_i k_j}}\]


All three metrics range from 0.0 (no overlap) to 1.0 (structural equivalence).

text:
Neighborhood Overlap in Directed Graphs

In directed networks, neighborhood overlap splits into:

Out-Similarity: Overlap in outgoing ties (pointing to the same others).
In-Similarity: Overlap in incoming ties (receiving nominations from the same others).

In Citation Networks (where paper \(A \rightarrow B\) means \(A\) cites \(B\)):

Bibliographic Coupling (Out-Similarity):

The number of references two papers have in common.
Measures similarity in theoretical foundations or sources.

Co-Citation (In-Similarity):

The frequency with which two papers are cited together by subsequent papers.
Measures how much the scientific community associates their ideas.

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
Directed Cosine Equations

Let \(n_{ij}^{out}\) / \(n_{ij}^{in}\) be the shared out-/in-neighbors, and \(k_i^{out}\) / \(k_i^{in}\) the out-/in-degrees.
Cosine Out-Similarity:

\[C_{ij}^{out} = \frac{n_{ij}^{out}}{\sqrt{k_i^{out} k_j^{out}}}\]

Cosine In-Similarity:

\[C_{ij}^{in} = \frac{n_{ij}^{in}}{\sqrt{k_i^{in} k_j^{in}}}\]

These formulas partition networks by highly specific sender and receiver roles.

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
Three Concepts of Equivalence

Beyond structural equivalence (sharing the exact same neighbors), there are three nested notions of relational position:

Structural Equivalence: Identical neighborhoods (\(N(u) = N(v)\)). Highly strict, same-neighbor rule.
Automorphic Equivalence: Globally symmetrical/interchangeable nodes. Nodes can be swapped without changing the graph structure.
Regular Equivalence: Connection to equivalent others. Focuses on general roles (e.g., all doctors connect to patients).

The Nested Hierarchy:

\(\text{Structural} \subseteq \text{Automorphic} \subseteq \text{Regular}\)

Let’s explore these definitions using a symmetrical 15-node network.

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
Symmetrical 15-Node Network



This 15-node network has:

Two star-like components centered at hubs \(B\) and \(K\).
Symmetrical leaf sets \(\{A,C,D,E\}\) and \(\{L,M,N,O\}\).
A tightly integrated central core \(\{F,G,H,I,J\}\).
\(G\) connects the core to hub \(B\); \(J\) connects the core to hub \(K\).
Let’s look at how we partition this network using the three equivalence criteria.

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
1. Structural Equivalence



Structural Equivalence Partition:

Requires connection to the exact same neighbors.
Groups:

Class 1: Leaf set \(\{A,C,D,E\}\) (connected only to \(B\)).
Class 2: Leaf set \(\{L,M,N,O\}\) (connected only to \(K\)).
All other nodes (colored separately) are in unique single-node classes.

Note: Symmetrical hubs \(B\) and \(K\) connect to different leaves, so they are not structurally equivalent!

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
2. Automorphic Equivalence



Automorphic Equivalence Partition:

Nodes that are globally interchangeable (symmetric swap).
groups nodes into four classes:

Leaves: \(\{A,C,D,E, L,M,N,O\}\)
Hubs: \(\{B,K\}\) (symmetric counterparts)
Core Bridges: \(\{G,J\}\) (gates to hubs)
Core Nodes: \(\{F,H,I\}\) (internally symmetric, no outside ties)

Successfully captures the structural similarity between hubs \(B\) and \(K\).

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
3. Regular Equivalence



Regular Equivalence Partition:

Connects to equivalent others (general roles).
Groups the 15 nodes into four roles:

Class 1 (Leaves): \(\{A,C,D,E, L,M,N,O\}\) (connect only to Hubs)
Class 2 (Hubs): \(\{B,K\}\) (connect to Leaves and Core Bridges)
Class 3 (Core Bridges): \(\{G,J\}\) (connect to Hubs and Core nodes)
Class 4 (Core Nodes): \(\{F,H,I\}\) (connect to Core Bridges and Core nodes)

Elegant and highly flexible role-mapping.

title: Graph Theory: Equivalence & Similarity
text:
Summary of Positional Concepts

Positions represent roles:

Unlike cohesive subgroups, actors do not need to connect to each other to be in the same position; they just need to connect to others similarly.

Structural Equivalence is the ideal limit:

Perfect row/column matching is highly elegant but rare in real social networks.

Structural Similarity relaxes the limit:

Distance metrics (Euclidean) and Overlap coefficients (Jaccard, Dice, Cosine) allow us to measure degrees of positional equivalence.

Directionality adds analytical depth:

Directed similarity splits into In-Similarity (Co-citation) and Out-Similarity (Bibliographic coupling), providing robust tools for citation and communication analysis.

title: Graph Theory: Blockmodeling
text:
The Correlation Distance (\(d^{corr}_{k,l}\))

Beyond Euclidean distance, we can measure structural similarity using the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (\(r_{kl}\) or \(d^{corr}_{kl}\)) between node vectors.
Compares row (or column) vectors and returns a value between \(-1.0\) and \(+1.0\):

\(+1.0\): Nodes are perfectly structurally equivalent.
Positive (\(> 0.0\)): Nodes are structurally similar.
Negative (\(< 0.0\)): Nodes are structurally dissimilar.
\(-1.0\): Nodes are completely different, pointing to completely disjoint sets of neighbors.

The formula is:

\[d^{corr}_{k, l} = \frac{\sum_j (a_{(k)j} - \overline{a}_{(k)j}) \times (a_{(l)j} - \overline{a}_{(l)j})}{\sqrt{\sum_j (a_{(k)j} - \overline{a}_{(k)j})^2 \times \sum_j (a_{(l)j} - \overline{a}_{(l)j})^2}}\]

title: Graph Theory: Blockmodeling
text:
Meaning of Row Means (\(\overline{a}_{(k)j}\))

What does \(\overline{a}_{(k)j}\) represent?

It is simply the average of the row elements for node \(k\).
\[\overline{a}_{(k)j} = \frac{\sum_j a_{kj}}{N}\]
Where \(N\) is the number of columns (the order of the graph).

For a binary adjacency matrix, the row mean is simply the node degree divided by the number of nodes:

Node \(A\) has ties to \(\{C, D\}\) in a 6-node network:
Vector \(a_{(A)j} = (0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0)\).
Average: \(\overline{a}_{(A)j} = \frac{2}{6} \approx 0.33\).
